items.prompt: What's the key difference between a unit test and an integration test?
choices: Unit tests are always shorter files than integration tests
A unit test checks one function/module in isolation; an integration test checks that multiple REAL components actually work together correctly (real contracts, not mocks)
There's no real difference — the terms are interchangeable
Integration tests can only be written in certain programming languages
items.explanation: Isolation is the defining property of a unit test — dependencies are typically mocked or absent. Integration tests specifically exercise real components together, which is what lets them catch contract mismatches a unit test's mocks would hide.
items.reference:
🧩 Unit

one function, isolated, mocked deps

🔗 Integration

real components, real contract

Why: isolation is what makes a unit test fast and precise; contacting real components is what lets an integration test catch a contract mismatch a mock would hide.
items.learnMore:
Unit vs. integration

A unit test isolates one function or module — dependencies are mocked or absent entirely, so a failure points at exactly one place. An integration test deliberately keeps at least one real dependency (a real database, a real running service) so it can catch the class of bug a unit test structurally can't see: two real components disagreeing about a shared contract, like a response shape or a field name.

Neither is 'better' — they answer different questions. A unit test answers 'is this logic correct in isolation?'. An integration test answers 'do these two real things actually agree with each other?'.

items.prompt: A test mocks out the database entirely and only checks that a function transforms input data correctly. What level is this test actually operating at, regardless of what folder it's filed in?
choices: Integration — it involves a database concept
Unit — nothing real is being contacted, so it's testing isolated logic no matter what it's named
E2E — any test involving data storage is end-to-end by definition
It's not a real test because it uses a mock
items.explanation: The level a test operates at is determined by what it actually touches, not its filename or folder. A fully mocked database means nothing real is contacted — that's unit-level isolation, whatever the test happens to be called.

Whether two real components' contracts actually agree with each other (e.g. does the real API return what the frontend expects)
Whether the function has good variable names
Whether the code will compile

items.prompt: Why does the test pyramid recommend MANY unit tests, FEWER integration tests, and the FEWEST e2e tests, rather than an equal number at each level?
choices: Because unit tests are considered more important than the other two levels

Because the shape reflects a real cost/confidence/specificity trade-off — unit tests are cheapest to write, run, and diagnose, while e2e tests are the most expensive per test, so the highest layer is reserved for the smallest number of critical, whole-flow checks
Because most testing frameworks technically only support a limited number of e2e tests
The shape is arbitrary convention with no underlying reasoning
items.explanation: The pyramid is explicit about this being a cost trade-off: e2e tests are slowest, most fragile, and least specific on failure — reserving them for a small number of critical flows, while relying on the cheaper unit level for the bulk of coverage, is what keeps the overall suite fast and diagnosable.
items.reference:
Many unit → some integration → few e2e: the shape follows cost, not habit.

Why: e2e is the slowest, most fragile, least specific-on-failure layer, so it's reserved for the smallest number of critical checks.
items.learnMore:
Why the pyramid isn't arbitrary

The pyramid's proportions encode a real cost/confidence/specificity trade-off. Unit tests are cheap to write, run in milliseconds, and point precisely at the broken function — so it makes sense to have many of them. E2E tests are expensive: slow, fragile (many moving parts), and vague on failure (a broken flow, not a broken line) — so it makes sense to have few, reserved for the flows that matter most.

The shape isn't a convention someone picked arbitrarily — it's what falls out of matching test volume to each level's actual cost.

items.prompt: If a team wrote exactly the same number of tests at each of the three levels (say, 100 unit, 100 integration, 100 e2e), what would be the practical downside compared to a properly-shaped pyramid with the same total?
choices: There is no downside — equal counts are always ideal
The suite would cost far more to run and diagnose than necessary, since 100 e2e tests carry e2e's full per-test cost (slow, fragile) for coverage a cheaper level could often provide just as well
The tests would fail to compile
Equal counts are impossible to configure in most test runners
items.explanation: Every e2e test carries a much higher runtime and fragility cost than a unit test. An equal split means paying that cost 100 times over instead of reserving it for the small number of checks that genuinely need a whole-flow test.

items.learnMore:
The inverted pyramid

An 'inverted pyramid' (or 'ice cream cone') is a suite with mostly e2e tests and very few unit tests — the opposite proportion from a healthy pyramid. It's a common trap because it feels thorough: lots of tests, driving the real app.

The problem is that this shape inherits e2e's costs (slow, fragile, imprecise-on-failure) at scale, without a corresponding increase in real bugs caught — the same coverage achieved with a well-shaped pyramid costs far less to run and trust.

items.prompt: Which of the following is a genuine downside of e2e tests, compared to unit tests?
choices: E2E tests are always written in a different programming language
E2E tests are slower, less specific about what actually broke on failure, and more fragile (fail for reasons unrelated to the real bug) than unit tests
E2E tests cannot be automated
E2E tests can only be run once per day
items.explanation: E2E tests trade speed, diagnostic precision, and stability for realism — they exercise the whole system the way a real user would, which is valuable, but it comes with real, predictable costs on those three other axes.
items.reference:
Speed

slowest

Specificity

Fragility

Why: e2e depends on the most moving parts — network, timing, rendering — all at once.
items.learnMore:
E2E's three costs

End-to-end tests drive the whole system the way a real user would, which is exactly what makes them the most realistic level — and also the most expensive on three separate axes: they're the slowest to run (seconds to minutes per test), the least specific on failure (a broken flow, not a broken line), and the most fragile (a real browser, real network calls, and real timing all have to cooperate for the test to even reach the assertion).

None of this makes e2e tests bad — it makes them expensive, which is the argument for using them sparingly, on the flows that matter most.

items.prompt: An e2e test and a unit test both fail on the same underlying bug. Which one, by itself, more precisely tells you WHERE the bug is?

The unit test — it isolates one function, so a failure points at exactly that function, while an e2e failure just says the overall flow broke
Neither test can ever indicate where a bug is located
They're always equally precise
items.explanation: Diagnostic precision is inversely related to how much a test exercises. A unit test's narrow scope is exactly what makes its failure point at one place; an e2e test's breadth is exactly what makes its failure vague.

items.prompt: A function computes tax on an order total using only its input arguments — no database, no network call. What level of test best fits it?
choices: E2E — tax calculations should always be tested through the full checkout flow
Unit — it's pure logic with no real dependencies, so an isolated test gives the fastest, most precise feedback
Integration — tax always involves an external system
It can't be tested at any level
items.explanation: A pure calculation with no I/O is the textbook case for a unit test: fast, isolated, and precise on failure — there's no real component to integrate with and no user-facing flow required to verify the math.
items.reference:
Ask: what would make this fail? Pure logic → unit. Real contract → integration. Whole flow → e2e.

Why: the failure cause determines the correct level, not habit or familiarity.
items.learnMore:
Picking the right level

The practical rule is to ask what specifically would make a given test fail, and let that answer pick the level: an isolated logic error belongs in a unit test, a mismatch between two real components' contracts belongs in an integration test, and a break in a critical whole user-facing flow belongs in a small number of e2e tests.

The mistake to avoid is defaulting to whichever level is most familiar or feels 'most thorough' rather than actually reasoning about what's being verified.

The unit/integration/e2e comparison spans four independent properties: speed, what's actually verified, failure specificity, and fragility. items.prompt: Per L2's decision flowchart, a test needs to verify that a pricing engine's real API returns the exact response shape the frontend expects, using a real running instance. What level does the flowchart route this to?

Integration — it's a mismatch question between two real components' contracts
E2E — any API interaction is automatically e2e
None of the levels apply
items.explanation: The flowchart's second branch is exactly this case: a real contract-mismatch question between two real components routes to integration, not unit (which would mock the API away) or e2e (which would test far more than the contract itself).

items.learnMore:
The decision procedure

L2's flowchart is a practical decision procedure, applied in order: is this a pure logic error in isolated code? Unit test. If not, is it a mismatch between two real components' contracts? Integration test. If not, is it a break in a critical, whole user-facing flow? E2E test, used sparingly.

Applying it consistently is what prevents defaulting to whichever level is most familiar or feels most thorough, instead of the level that actually matches the failure being guarded against.

items.learnMore:
Testing at the wrong level wastes effort

Choosing a level higher than what's actually needed doesn't add safety — it adds cost for no corresponding benefit. A pure logic edge case doesn't need a real browser to verify; a heavily-mocked 'integration' test that contacts nothing real can't verify a real contract no matter how it's labeled.

The discipline is matching the level to what's actually being verified, in both directions — not under-testing critical flows, and not over-testing things a cheaper level already covers.

items.prompt: Implement `classifyTestLevel({ isPureLogic, touchesRealComponent, drivesRealBrowser })`, encoding L2's decision procedure: if `drivesRealBrowser` is true, return "e2e". Otherwise, if `touchesRealComponent` is true, return "integration". Otherwise (pure, isolated logic), return "unit".

tests.description: pure logic with no real dependencies is a unit test
tests.expr: expect(classifyTestLevel({ isPureLogic: true, touchesRealComponent: false, drivesRealBrowser: false })).toBe('unit')

tests.description: touching a real component (real DB/service) is an integration test
tests.expr: expect(classifyTestLevel({ isPureLogic: false, touchesRealComponent: true, drivesRealBrowser: false })).toBe('integration')

tests.description: driving a real browser is an e2e test, even if it also touches real components
tests.expr: expect(classifyTestLevel({ isPureLogic: false, touchesRealComponent: true, drivesRealBrowser: true })).toBe('e2e')

items.explanation: This mirrors L2's decision flowchart exactly: the most expensive/broadest condition (a real browser driving the whole flow) takes precedence, since an e2e test by definition also exercises real component integration along the way — the level is determined by the widest scope of what's actually being verified, not just any single property in isolation.
items.reference:
Widest scope wins: drives a real browser → e2e; else touches a real component → integration; else → unit.

Why: an e2e test also exercises real integration along the way, so the broadest true condition determines the level.
items.learnMore:
Encoding the decision procedure in code

L2's flowchart can be written as straightforward conditional logic: check the broadest-scope condition first (does it drive a real browser through a whole flow?), then the next-broadest (does it touch a real component?), and only fall through to 'unit' if neither applies.

The ordering matters because a test that drives a real browser almost always also touches real components along the way — checking the widest scope first is what keeps the classification correct rather than ambiguous.

items.prompt: An e2e test fails intermittently. Per L3's failure modes, should this be treated with the same confidence as a failing unit test (i.e., assume it's a real regression)?
choices: Yes — any test failure should always be treated as a confirmed regression

No — e2e tests have the highest fragility of the three levels (most moving parts: network, timing, rendering), so an intermittent failure needs actual triage to distinguish a real regression from an environment/timing flake, unlike a unit test which almost never fails for unrelated reasons
No, because e2e test failures should always be ignored
Yes, but only if the test has failed more than three times in a row
items.explanation: L2's fragility comparison and L3's failure modes both point to this directly: e2e's dependence on the most moving parts makes intermittent failures common for reasons unrelated to the actual code, which is exactly why they warrant investigation before being trusted as strongly as a unit test failure.
items.reference:
An e2e failure needs triage before it's trusted like a unit test failure.

Why: e2e depends on the most moving parts, so intermittent failures are common for reasons unrelated to the real bug.
items.learnMore:
Flaky e2e failures need triage

Because e2e tests depend on the most moving parts — network, timing, rendering — an intermittent failure is common for reasons that have nothing to do with the code under test. A failing unit test almost never has this problem, since there's little external to fail unrelated to the logic itself.

The practical implication: an e2e failure warrants actual investigation (was this a real regression, or a timing/environment flake?) before being treated with the same confidence as a unit test failure.

items.prompt: A team's policy is to automatically re-run any failing e2e test once, and treat it as passing if the re-run succeeds, without ever looking closer. What real risk does this policy accept?
choices: None — this is always the correct way to handle e2e flakiness

It risks silently accepting real regressions that happen to also be intermittent (e.g. a race condition introduced by the change itself), by treating any pass-on-retry as automatically a flake rather than sometimes investigating why
It makes the test suite run slower, which is the only downside
It has no downside since unit tests would catch anything real anyway
items.explanation: Blind auto-retry conflates two different situations: an unrelated environment flake, and a real bug that happens to manifest intermittently (like a race condition). Treating every retry-pass as "just a flake" without investigation can let genuine regressions through.

items.prompt: A test labeled "integration test" mocks out the discount service entirely and only checks that the frontend calls a function with the right arguments. Per L3's failure modes, what's the problem?
choices: Nothing — mocking is always appropriate for integration tests

It's a unit test wearing an integration test's name — since nothing real is actually being contacted, it can't catch a real contract mismatch between the frontend and the actual service, which is the entire point of testing at the integration level
The problem is that it doesn't run fast enough
The problem is that it should be an e2e test instead
items.explanation: L3 explicitly warns against this: heavy mocking in a nominally-integration test defeats its purpose, since integration tests exist specifically to verify real components' contracts actually match — a mock just returns whatever shape was assumed when it was written, which is exactly the assumption a real integration test is meant to check.
items.reference:
Mocking out the real dependency turns an "integration test" into a unit test in disguise.

Why: a mock returns whatever shape was assumed when it was written — it can't catch a real mismatch.
items.learnMore:
The fake-integration-test trap

A test that mocks out every real dependency but is still labeled "integration" doesn't get integration's benefit — it's a unit test wearing the wrong name. The entire value of an integration test comes from contacting something real, so it can catch the case where the frontend's assumption about a response shape and the backend's actual behavior have quietly diverged.

A mock is only ever as accurate as the assumption baked into it when it was written — it structurally cannot detect that assumption going stale.

items.prompt: The real discount-code service changes its response field from `percent` to `discountPercent`, but nobody updates the frontend. A heavily-mocked "integration" test still passes. What does this reveal?
choices: That the change was safe, since the test still passed
That the mock encodes the OLD assumption (`percent`) and never noticed the real service changed — exactly the class of bug a genuine integration test (contacting the real service) would have caught
That the frontend code must be broken in an unrelated way
That mocked tests are always more reliable than real ones
items.explanation: A mock is frozen at whatever assumption it was written with. When the real contract changes, the mock doesn't know — it just keeps returning the old shape, so the test keeps passing while the real integration silently breaks. This is precisely why integration tests need to contact something real.

items.prompt: Implement `estimateSuiteRuntimeMs({ unitCount, integrationCount, e2eCount }, { unitMs, integrationMs, e2eMs })`, returning the total estimated runtime in milliseconds: each count times its corresponding per-test time, summed across all three levels.

tests.description: all zero counts gives zero runtime
tests.expr: expect(estimateSuiteRuntimeMs({ unitCount: 0, integrationCount: 0, e2eCount: 0 }, { unitMs: 50, integrationMs: 1500, e2eMs: 12000 })).toBe(0)

tests.description: sums each level's count times its per-test time
tests.expr: expect(estimateSuiteRuntimeMs({ unitCount: 10, integrationCount: 2, e2eCount: 1 }, { unitMs: 50, integrationMs: 1000, e2eMs: 10000 })).toBe(12500)

tests.description: a large e2e count dominates even a much larger unit count
tests.expr: expect(estimateSuiteRuntimeMs({ unitCount: 400, integrationCount: 0, e2eCount: 10 }, { unitMs: 50, integrationMs: 1500, e2eMs: 12000 })).toBe(140000)

items.explanation: This is a direct sum of count × time per level. It's worth noticing how little it takes for e2e to dominate: in the third test, 400 unit tests at 50ms each only cost 20,000ms total, while just 10 e2e tests at 12,000ms each cost 120,000ms — six times more, from a fraction of the test count.
items.reference:
total runtime = (unitCount × unitMs) + (integrationCount × integrationMs) + (e2eCount × e2eMs)

Why: the same math drives the unit's interactive demo — e2e's per-test cost dominates the total even with few tests.
items.learnMore:
Estimating suite runtime

Total suite runtime is the sum, across each level, of test count times average per-test time. Because e2e's per-test time is orders of magnitude larger than a unit test's, even a small e2e count can dominate the total — which is the concrete, measurable version of "the inverted pyramid is expensive."

This is the exact relationship the unit's interactive demo lets you explore by dragging the percentage of e2e tests.

items.prompt: E2E tests are the most realistic of the three levels — they drive the system the way a real user would. Why does the pyramid still recommend using them sparingly rather than as the primary testing strategy?
choices: Because realism doesn't cancel out cost — the same real browser, real network, and real timing that make e2e realistic also make it the slowest and most fragile level, so it's reserved for a small set of critical flows
Because e2e tests are technically unable to catch most bugs
Because most companies don't have the budget for e2e tests at all
Realism is actually irrelevant to test quality
items.explanation: Realism and cost are two separate properties, not opposites — e2e is both the most realistic AND the most expensive, and the pyramid's advice to use it sparingly is about managing that cost, not about doubting its realism.
items.reference:
E2E is the most realistic level, but reserved for a small, deliberate set of critical flows.

Why: realism doesn't cancel out cost — the two are separate axes.
items.learnMore:
Why e2e stays sparing even though it's the most realistic

E2E tests are the closest thing to how a real user actually experiences the system — which can make it tempting to lean on them heavily, since they feel like the strongest evidence something works. But realism and cost are separate axes: the same properties that make e2e realistic (a real browser, real network calls, real timing) are exactly what make it slow and fragile.

The discipline is reserving e2e for a small, deliberately chosen set of critical flows — checkout, signup, payment — rather than letting its realism justify using it everywhere a cheaper level would already answer the question.

items.prompt: A team decides that because e2e tests are the most convincing evidence a feature works, every new feature should get a dedicated e2e test in addition to its unit and integration tests. What's the risk in applying this uniformly?
choices: There is no risk — more e2e coverage is always strictly better

It reintroduces the inverted-pyramid cost at scale: the suite grows slower and more fragile with every feature, even for features whose risk was already fully covered by cheaper, more precise unit and integration tests
E2E tests cannot be written for most features

items.explanation: Applying 'e2e for everything' uniformly is the inverted pyramid by another name — it treats e2e's realism as if it were free, when the same coverage a lower level already provides doesn't need to be paid for again at e2e's much higher cost.
